RAND FREEFALL

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
While the rand has hit an all time low and it's good news for exporters, importers and ordinary citizens will be feeling the brunt. How will we be hardest hit?

Summary:
On Monday, the rand reached its lowest level ever against the dollar of 14,01 and economists say South Africa will feel the effects as the rand continues to come under pressure against major currencies. What does this mean for the ordinary South African?

Further information:
It's also the lowest the rand has been against the pound as possible hikes in the US and Chinese markets further create uncertainty.
Reserve Bank Governor, Lsetja Kganyago has said that a further fall in the rand is not necessarily a bad thing and the currency should be allowed to play its role as a shock absorber, but not all economists agree with him. The Governor said the rand depreciation was part of a global foreign exchange rebalancing, it need not be a worry.

Economists expect the weaker rand is likely to fuel inflation, putting pressure on the central bank to raise domestic rates further despite an economy struggling to grow in the face of South Africa's worst power crisis in seven years.

Eskom has implemented load shedding on 99 days this year, the legacy of a decade of underinvestment in new generating capacity. Load shedding has forced mines and factories to scale back production at a time when rising wage demands boost costs and commodity prices plunge.

The rand has been on a losing streak since 2011, partly due to mounting domestic woes and investor disenchantment with emerging banks.

Pressure on the currency has intensified this year as the SA Reserve Bank prepares to raise interest rates, commodity prices that account for more than half of South Africa’s exports dive and the Chinese economy slows.

But for corporate South Africa, the tumbling rand has been both a blessing and a curse: while it has been a windfall for ining houses, it has also saddled domestic manufacturers and retailers with higher costs and weaker consumer demand.

The currency free fall has left a raft of companies scrambling to contain the damage. On export side, it leads to higher inflation, higher fuel costs and higher capital goods costs. The effect is even worse for companies focused on the domestic economy, who are stuck with higher costs without the benefit of foreign exchange revenue.

But what does all this mean for us - consumers?

South Africans might find filling their food baskets a tough task in coming months as the prices of household staples – including maize meal, meat, eggs and diary products – are set to rise.

The agriculture industry has been beset by a drought that has devastated output and raised the need for imports – this while the rand has been battered on the markets and trading at a record low, making imports both unattractive and expensive.

Consumers may not feel the pinch of the developments at retail level immediately – it takes about four months for maize prize increases to trickle down to actual products such as maize meal and samp and the price lag for poultry, meat and diary products is slightly longer and could materialise in the next six months.

Lags occur because of the time it takes farmers to produce maize and the production process it undergoes before it hits shelves. A similar phenomenon happens with meat and poultry, which is associated with the time it takes to rear the animals for slaughter and packaging.

And how is it going with car sales companies for example, big and small businesses?

Press Release:


Rand Free Fall
At the end of August, the rand dropped to its lowest level ever against the US dollar and has only marginally recovered since. It’s good news for exporters, but importers and ordinary consumers are still to face the brunt of our currency’s free fall. The rand has been on a losing streak since 2011 due to mounting domestic woes and a lack of investor confidence, but economists believe businesses and individuals will really feel the pinch in months to come. Is there hope on the horizon for overstretched consumers? Carte Blanche investigates.

RAND FREEFALL

PRODUCER: ESTé DE KLERK

How much value do you really get for your Rand?
Or rather, are you able to buy a burger with some loose change in your purse?
Well, if you are at fast-food restaurant, McDonalds, you’ll be able to order a Big Mac with R30 AND get change – South Africa’s is the sixth cheapest in the world.

BONGANI LINK: One of the best ways to test our currency is through the humble Big Mac. Bought in SA in rands, it will cost you just over R26, in New York $4,79 and that is where it gets really interesting, because if you buy it in rands in the US it is the equivalent of R65 and bought here with dollars, it will cost you just over two.

One US Dollar will give an American tourist a little more than thirteen rands.
In South Africa - with only one dollar – they’ll be able to buy a 2L coldrink, a litre of milk, a pack of Rooibos Tea OR half dozen eggs… And for just over a dollar, they can buy a tube of toothpaste and a kilogram of maize meal.
But for R1, South Africans will not be able to buy anything really – at least not any of your bare necessities.

BONGANI LINK: There are a number of things one can do to stretch the rand including cutting down on electricity and fuel consumption and even entertainment, but no one can stop eating and this is where most consumers are going to feel the pinch when the price of basic food stuffs like maize.

The ongoing drought has necessitated the import of 750-thousand tons of maize. There is also a shortage of 1,8 million tons of wheat. The weaker rand adds inflationary pressures and the increased cost trickles down from the manufacturer to retail level – directly affecting our pockets and hitting the poor the hardest, says economist Xhanti Payi.

XHANTI: We are net-importers of our food, which means as soon as the rand collapses, the prices of food hits the poor person much quicker, because that is what they spend most of their money on.

Our currency is sick and the economy is wavering.
At the worst level it’s ever been against the US dollar, the Rand is particularly vulnerable because it’s one of the world’s most highly traded emerging market currencies.

XHANTI PAYI: People are now sort of moving away from these markets – they are investing a lot in emerging markets, they are taking that money away and looking for better, safer and more stable places like the US.

South Africa’s economy relies on the sale of commodities… and rising fears of an economic slowdown in China – a major source of demand – have contributed to the Rand’s volatility.

XHANTI PAYI: We are all grouped together with China as an emerging market, so whatever people perceive about China, they would tend to also think that about SA and countries like Russia, Brazil, like Russia.

But we have much more to offer the world than only our commodities – South Africa is breathtakingly beautiful and we should take advantage of the abundance our country can offer, says John Ridler, PR manager of Thompsons Travel.

BONGANI: How familiar are South Africans with what this country actually has to offer?

JOHN RIDLER: Not as familiar as they should be. [01:07:32.13] I think we are not and we should be doing more to attract other African countries to visit us because I think there is a huge potential there.

Despite the country’s restrictive new visa regulations and foreign investors’ seemingly dwindling confidence in our country, more and more international tourists will flock to South Africa – thanks to our weaker Rand.

For less than what they may spend on a local holiday in their own countries, in South Africa tourists may take to the bush on a real African Safari to witness the Big Five; or see penguins at Simonstown as they waddle along the beach, relax in Cape Town, witness spectacular Table Mountain or visit one of the vineyards near Franschoek.

So South Africa is really a good deal for their money.

BONGANI: Is the rand in freefall?

XHANTI PAYI: Freefall is a very big word. On a longterm-basis it is weakening, it is probably not a bad thing, so basically, people can now come and visit and stay in hotels for cheaper prices without us actually doing anything…

Hotel prices may vary depending on demand at the time of booking
So let’s make a quick comparison: Johannesburg, Paris and London. Tonight at the Hilton Hotel in Jo’burg, a standard room for two will cost R2200 per night.
For almost double the price, South Africans, can get a room at the Hilton Paris Opéra – costing: 269 Euro, or R4050;
while a night at the Hilton London Paddington, will set you back 152 Pounds Sterling, equivalent to R3140.
So this quick look at various tourist capitals reveals how much South Africans will have to cough up if they want to stay in a hotel on par with what they can normally afford here.

LINK SUN1 HOTEL: When it comes to affordable accommodation, this is about as good as it gets, because at a hotel like this for just under R500 you can get a room sleeping up to 3 people with its own bathroom. In Europe for example you would be lucky to get a bed in a dormitory for that amount.

John says the phones are ringing off the hook with South Africans scrambling to try and cancel or change overseas holidays booked and paid for.

JOHN RIDLER: the trend would be to send us an itinerary to quote on and it would be quite grand, and within minutes it’s back and they say where can we cut costs. We would cut down the number of days, or the quality of the hotel.

BONGANI: So people are still prepared to travel they just want it cheaper.

JOHN RIDLER: Potential travelers are saying we will pay for the ticket now and we will pay for the land arrangements later, they are hedging their bets. They would say has the hotel got full English breakfast, because you can tank up on a full English breakfast, one less meal to pay for for the day.

Visas needed to traverse the world, will also now cost us more. This means a potential loss of business for Quentin van den Berg, owner of Visas Direct, a business that secures visas on the traveler’s behalf.

QUENTIN VAN DEN BERG: You pay according to the exchange rate what their fee is – Euro’s, Pounds, Dollars. People are going to have to fork out more for the embassy and less for the service provider.

But, if your overseas trip is already booked, save a bit more now, says John – and - be streetwise.

JOHN RIDLER: You would have to learn the tricks of the trade, learn to do take aways, find places off the high street. I mean, I recently had a coffee in a smart restaurant and it was R250 - now that’s eye watering.

BONGANI: I mean I know there is very different destinations, there is a lot of the numbers will vary, but what will a modest overseas holiday cost you know the average family?

JOHN: Well if you went to one of the Islands Mauritius or lets say Thailand, you could be paying R15 000 out of season as much as R25 000 in season, but the minuet you go to the UK or even to the United States, the price goes up quite substantially, so in the UK you will be paying between R35 000 and R40 000 for a seven-day holiday to the United States, possibly another R5 000 more than that.

But if you had to waive such an overseas trip good-bye because it’s now too expensive, what do you say about a family-roadtrip from the Kruger to Cape Town?
And before the rand gets any worse, now would be a good time to buy a new car, says Kia Motors CEO, Ray Levin.

RAY LEVIN: I think for a consumer now is the best time to buy a car, if you just think about where the rand dollar is and where we have purchased our dollars you are probably looking at a 12 to 15% increase by January February next year. We hedge our dollars out so we are fairly comfortable until december January this year, and hopefully the dollar will come back and we will be able to price our cars accordingly.

Bongani: But are car purchases dropping are car sales.

RAY LEVIN. We look at 1 in 3 applicators, just over 1 in 3 applications a week approved and even slightly worse than one in four have been taken up, so affordability is a major problem.

One little pleasure we as South Africans can at least still afford is that special brew we love and need so much.

BONGANI LINK: That is easily one of the best cups of coffee I have ever tasted. In Johannesburg and surrounds, you would pay around R25 for a similar size coffee. Go overseas, you will pay double that. And surely that means we are scoring, right? Not necessarily.

Wayne Burrows is the owner of Urban Grind, a speciality coffee bean shop in Parkhurst, Johannesburg. For the past fourteen years, he’s been importing green coffee beans from all over the world, roasting it and selling it to restaurants and coffee shops across South Africa.

BONGANI: So why are we paying less for coffee?

WAYNE BURROWS: The consumer over the last five years has been paying the same amount of money for a cup of coffee, but our exchange rate is now different. It’s the most traded soft commodity on the stock exchange, you know, its hedged at a specific rand to dollar price. In order to give you the same cup of coffee at the same price, I am going to have to put a lesser grade coffee into that blend.

But we are going to have to fork out more for medication.
Discovery Health CEO, dr. Jonathan Broomberg says consumers are likely to scale down on specific plans of medical aids.

DR. JONATHAN BROOMBERG: ….there is a buying-down phenomenon, but not a dropping-out. Medicines and a large items…

Twenty-nine year old Ryan de Klerk, now has to work twice as hard to afford his
expenses and his studies in 3D-animation through an international University in California. He lectures in animation at two institutions and has his own web-design business.

RYAN DE KLERK: My day starts at 5 in the morning and ends at 10 at night, seven days a week. I had to sacrifice time sleeping, time with family and friends…just to get by.

Since the rand tumbled, the cost of his studies has shot up by R2000 and is now R9000 a month.

And economists warn that it will get worse before it gets better.

XHANTI PAYI: We see that the things that are happening in China are going to go on for a little bit longer. It can drop as far as 18/20, but it will come back.

BONGANI LINK: So quite clearly, … there is one thing we can do and that is manage how we are perceived and that is ultimately a question of leadership.

XHANTI PAYI: Government needs to say …..as strongly as we should.

Summary: On Monday, the rand reached its lowest level ever against the dollar of 14,01 and economists say South Africa will feel the effects as the rand continues to come under pressure against major currencies. What does this mean for the ordinary South African? Further information: It's also the lowest the rand has been against the pound as possible hikes in the US and Chinese markets further create uncertainty. Reserve Bank Governor, Lsetja Kganyago has said that a further fall in the rand is not necessarily a bad thing and the currency should be allowed to play its role as a shock absorber, but not all economists agree with him. The Governor said the rand depreciation was part of a global foreign exchange rebalancing, it need not be a worry. Economists expect the weaker rand is likely to fuel inflation, putting pressure on the central bank to raise domestic rates further despite an economy struggling to grow in the face of South Africa's worst power crisis in seven years. Eskom has implemented load shedding on 99 days this year, the legacy of a decade of underinvestment in new generating capacity. Load shedding has forced mines and factories to scale back production at a time when rising wage demands boost costs and commodity prices plunge. The rand has been on a losing streak since 2011, partly due to mounting domestic woes and investor disenchantment with emerging banks. Pressure on the currency has intensified this year as the SA Reserve Bank prepares to raise interest rates, commodity prices that account for more than half of South Africa’s exports dive and the Chinese economy slows. But for corporate South Africa, the tumbling rand has been both a blessing and a curse: while it has been a windfall for ining houses, it has also saddled domestic manufacturers and retailers with higher costs and weaker consumer demand. The currency free fall has left a raft of companies scrambling to contain the damage. On export side, it leads to higher inflation, higher fuel costs and higher capital goods costs. The effect is even worse for companies focused on the domestic economy, who are stuck with higher costs without the benefit of foreign exchange revenue. But what does all this mean for us - consumers? South Africans might find filling their food baskets a tough task in coming months as the prices of household staples – including maize meal, meat, eggs and diary products – are set to rise. The agriculture industry has been beset by a drought that has devastated output and raised the need for imports – this while the rand has been battered on the markets and trading at a record low, making imports both unattractive and expensive. Consumers may not feel the pinch of the developments at retail level immediately – it takes about four months for maize prize increases to trickle down to actual products such as maize meal and samp and the price lag for poultry, meat and diary products is slightly longer and could materialise in the next six months. Lags occur because of the time it takes farmers to produce maize and the production process it undergoes before it hits shelves. A similar phenomenon happens with meat and poultry, which is associated with the time it takes to rear the animals for slaughter and packaging. And how is it going with car sales companies for example, big and small businesses? metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): While the rand has hit an all time low and it's good news for exporters, importers and ordinary citizens will be feeling the brunt. How will we be hardest hit?
metadata.Summary: On Monday, the rand reached its lowest level ever against the dollar of 14,01 and economists say South Africa will feel the effects as the rand continues to come under pressure against major currencies. What does this mean for the ordinary South African?
metadata.Further information: It's also the lowest the rand has been against the pound as possible hikes in the US and Chinese markets further create uncertainty. Reserve Bank Governor, Lsetja Kganyago has said that a further fall in the rand is not necessarily a bad thing and the currency should be allowed to play its role as a shock absorber, but not all economists agree with him. The Governor said the rand depreciation was part of a global foreign exchange rebalancing, it need not be a worry. Economists expect the weaker rand is likely to fuel inflation, putting pressure on the central bank to raise domestic rates further despite an economy struggling to grow in the face of South Africa's worst power crisis in seven years. Eskom has implemented load shedding on 99 days this year, the legacy of a decade of underinvestment in new generating capacity. Load shedding has forced mines and factories to scale back production at a time when rising wage demands boost costs and commodity prices plunge. The rand has been on a losing streak since 2011, partly due to mounting domestic woes and investor disenchantment with emerging banks. Pressure on the currency has intensified this year as the SA Reserve Bank prepares to raise interest rates, commodity prices that account for more than half of South Africa’s exports dive and the Chinese economy slows. But for corporate South Africa, the tumbling rand has been both a blessing and a curse: while it has been a windfall for ining houses, it has also saddled domestic manufacturers and retailers with higher costs and weaker consumer demand. The currency free fall has left a raft of companies scrambling to contain the damage. On export side, it leads to higher inflation, higher fuel costs and higher capital goods costs. The effect is even worse for companies focused on the domestic economy, who are stuck with higher costs without the benefit of foreign exchange revenue. But what does all this mean for us - consumers? South Africans might find filling their food baskets a tough task in coming months as the prices of household staples – including maize meal, meat, eggs and diary products – are set to rise. The agriculture industry has been beset by a drought that has devastated output and raised the need for imports – this while the rand has been battered on the markets and trading at a record low, making imports both unattractive and expensive. Consumers may not feel the pinch of the developments at retail level immediately – it takes about four months for maize prize increases to trickle down to actual products such as maize meal and samp and the price lag for poultry, meat and diary products is slightly longer and could materialise in the next six months. Lags occur because of the time it takes farmers to produce maize and the production process it undergoes before it hits shelves. A similar phenomenon happens with meat and poultry, which is associated with the time it takes to rear the animals for slaughter and packaging. And how is it going with car sales companies for example, big and small businesses?
